overview: Visigothic history connects mobile Gothic groups with kingdoms centred first on Toulouse and later on Toledo. This imported 400 to 600 record changes from a Balkan snapshot to territory in Gaul and Iberia. Those outlines should not suggest one fixed homeland or a continuously occupied border; the people and their political institutions changed over time.

periods.title: Across the Roman world
periods.summary: Gothic groups moved from the Balkans through Italy into Gaul.

periods.title: The Toulouse kingdom
periods.summary: A kingdom developed in southwestern Gaul and extended its influence into Iberia.

periods.title: Power shifts toward Iberia
periods.summary: After defeat by the Franks, Visigothic royal power became centred in Iberia.

items.text: At Toulouse, excavators found an imposing complex beside the Roman city wall, interpreted as the probable royal palace. It included a vestibule, corridors and connected rooms, one with an apse. New rulers adapted a Roman city rather than building everything on an empty site.

Monumental buildings along the Garonne included churches and a rectangular structure with a surrounding gallery. Its purpose remains uncertain, possibly funerary. The arrangement suggests coordinated building projects, showing how rulers and religious institutions could change the appearance of a city.

Brooches, earrings and belt buckles preserve traces of personal dress in Toulouse and its countryside. Some burial grounds appear to have served both local inhabitants and newcomers. Shared places complicate any simple picture of two populations living completely separate lives.

sections.title: A small object for a familiar task

items.text: Bone combs from rural estates in southwestern Gaul have a single row of teeth, rounded backs and decoration made of small circles. Comparable forms occur around the Black Sea. Such connections help archaeologists investigate movement and cultural contacts through an object used for everyday grooming.

At the site identified as Recópolis near Zorita de los Canes, excavated houses contained rectangular rooms arranged around courtyards. Rooms served living, cooking, storage and animal-keeping functions. This gives a much fuller picture of domestic space than a palace plan alone.

The houses used stone footings, plastered earth walls and tiled roofs, with floors of packed clay or lime mortar. Excavators recovered cooking pots, jugs, bowls and bottles, including some imported North African ceramics. Ordinary households participated in wider Mediterranean exchanges.

The settlement used both an aqueduct and cisterns. The aqueduct collected spring water outside the city, probably supplying its highest area. Having an aqueduct does not establish that every house had running water; different parts of the settlement used different arrangements.

Workshops made glass tableware, including cups and plates, while a metalworking area yielded moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metal waste. These finds reveal specialised crafts and the tools behind finished objects, from shaping a vessel to weighing valuable material.

At Mérida, some mosaics remained in use, were repaired or were newly made well into the sixth century. A change of ruler did not instantly erase older skills or tastes. The museum’s material shows how late Roman and Visigothic-period urban life overlapped.

Mérida’s surviving objects include pottery, church sculpture and many funerary inscriptions. These materials illuminate different activities: preparing food, decorating worship spaces and commemorating the dead. Much of this city’s evidence concerns its wider population, rather than identifying the ancestry of each maker.

sections.title: A tiny Latin message of power

items.text: A gold coin of Reccared I, who ruled from 586 to 601, bears the Latin word “REX”, meaning “king”. The coin found at Begastri was minted at Toledo. Its lettering also names that mint as TOLETO, a compact declaration of authority on a small object.

This tremissis weighs about 1.48 grams and measures 18 millimetres across. Its royal portrait appears on both faces. The coin provides evidence for gold-working, monetary standards and royal representation, though it does not tell us what every household could afford to buy.

ending.text: The imported interval ends in 600, but the Toledo kingdom continued into the eighth century. Muslim-led conquest beginning in 711 overthrew its central monarchy. Communities and inherited traditions continued under new political arrangements.

sources.note: Overview by emeritus medieval-history professor; used for broad movement, Toulouse/Toledo phases and 711 conquest, not older essentialist ethnic characterisations or detailed conquest legends.
